subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Working from maquette to final piece

questions.q: Carving is best described as which type of sculptural process?
options: A subtractive process, removing material from a block
An additive process, building material up
A casting process, pouring liquid into a mould
An assembly process, joining found objects
questions.explain: Carving removes (subtracts) material such as stone or wood to reveal a form.

questions.q: Which material is most commonly associated with the process of modelling?
questions.explain: Modelling is an additive process using pliable materials such as clay or wax.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an armature in sculpture?
options: To provide an internal support or framework for modelled material
To glaze the surface of a finished piece
To colour the surface of bronze
questions.explain: An armature is a rigid internal skeleton that supports soft modelling material such as clay.

questions.q: In sculpture, what is a maquette?
options: A small preliminary scale model of a proposed sculpture
A tool used for carving stone
The base or plinth a sculpture stands on
questions.explain: A maquette is a small rough model made to plan and test ideas before the final piece.

questions.q: A sculpture described as 'in the round' is one that is:
options: Designed to be viewed from all sides
questions.explain: Sculpture in the round is free-standing and intended to be seen from every angle.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a relief sculpture?
options: Forms that project from and remain attached to a flat background
A free-standing figure viewable from all sides
A sculpture powered by a motor
questions.explain: In relief the sculpted form is raised from a flat surface rather than being fully free-standing.

questions.q: In sculpture, the term 'negative space' refers to:
options: The empty space around and within a form
The solid mass of the object
The base the sculpture rests on
The rough surface texture of a material
questions.explain: Negative space is the empty area surrounding or enclosed by the solid (positive) form.

questions.q: The construction or assemblage method of making sculpture mainly involves:
options: Joining together separate materials or found objects
Cutting away from a single solid block
Pouring molten metal into a mould
questions.explain: Construction and assemblage build a sculpture by combining and fixing together separate parts.

questions.q: The traditional bronze casting method known as 'cire perdue' is more commonly called:
questions.explain: Cire perdue, or lost-wax casting, uses a wax model that is melted out to leave a mould for metal.

questions.q: A kinetic sculpture is one that:
options: Is designed to hang on a wall
questions.explain: Kinetic sculpture includes actual movement, whether driven by air, motors or the viewer.

questions.q: A student is planning a large final sculpture and wants to test how its proportions and balance work in three dimensions before committing. What should they make first?
questions.explain: A maquette lets the student trial form, proportion and balance cheaply before scaling up.

questions.q: The coloured surface film applied to or formed on bronze sculpture is called a:
questions.explain: A patina is the surface colouring on bronze, which may form naturally or be applied deliberately.

questions.q: In three-dimensional work, 'form' is best understood as:
options: A shape with height, width and depth
The colour applied to a surface
The type of tool used to carve
questions.explain: Form is a three-dimensional shape possessing volume, with height, width and depth.

questions.q: A student shapes a figure by removing material from a bar of soap with a knife. Which process are they using?
questions.explain: Cutting material away from a solid block is a subtractive process, i.e. carving.

questions.q: Why must an artist scale up a maquette carefully when making the final piece?
options: To keep the proportions of the original design accurate
To reduce the amount of planning needed
questions.explain: Careful, measured scaling preserves the proportions and relationships worked out in the maquette.

questions.q: In a sculpture, the 'positive space' refers to:
options: The solid mass of the form itself
The empty gaps around the form
The lighting used to display it
questions.explain: Positive space is the actual solid form, as opposed to the empty negative space around it.

questions.q: A student wants to fire a solid clay sculpture in a kiln safely. What is the most important precaution?
options: Hollow it out and ensure walls of even thickness
Make the walls as thick as possible
Fire it while the clay is still wet
Coat it in wax before firing
questions.explain: Hollowing the form with even, thin walls lets trapped air and moisture escape, preventing it exploding.

questions.q: An artist designs a sculpture in which the empty gaps between the metal rods are just as important to the composition as the rods themselves. Which concept are they exploiting?
questions.explain: Using the empty gaps as an active part of the composition is a deliberate use of negative space.
